pointers.sentence: A permission prints as its content type and its name, `"Fleet | ship | Can change ship"`, and `Permission.user_perm_str`, new in 6.1, gives the string a check takes, `"fleet.change_ship"` (`django/contrib/auth/models.py:Permission`).
A permission's natural key is its codename, its application's label and its model's name (`django/contrib/auth/models.py:PermissionManager.get_by_natural_key`).
The serialization documentation gives the reason one is wanted: migrate makes these rows, so their primary keys depend on how and when it ran (`docs/topics/serialization.txt`).

The group model is a unique name and a many-to-many field of permissions, with its name as its natural key; its docstring calls it a generic way of categorizing users, for permissions or any other label (`django/contrib/auth/models.py:Group`).

Both name their reverse accessor `"user_set"` and their reverse lookup `"user"`, where a model's own name would otherwise go, so a query from a group or a permission to its users, such as `ModelBackend.with_perm`'s, reads the same whatever the user model is called (`django/contrib/auth/models.py:PermissionsMixin`).

The first backend to answer true makes the answer yes, and one that raises `PermissionDenied` makes it no at once, the docstring's way for a backend to cut the checks short; after the last, it is no (`django/contrib/auth/models.py:PermissionsMixin.has_perm`, `django/contrib/auth/models.py:_user_has_perm`).

The three getters, `PermissionsMixin.get_user_permissions`, `PermissionsMixin.get_group_permissions` and `PermissionsMixin.get_all_permissions`, have no shortcut for the superuser: `_user_get_permissions` returns the union of the sets of every backend that has the method (`django/contrib/auth/models.py:_user_get_permissions`).

`BaseBackend` answers `BaseBackend.has_perm` by membership of the union of its two getters, which give empty sets; it has no `has_module_perms`, which is asked only of backends that have one (`django/contrib/auth/backends.py:BaseBackend`).

`ModelBackend.get_all_permissions` keeps their union under `"_perm_cache"`, and `ModelBackend.has_perm` answers whether the user is active and the string is in it (`django/contrib/auth/backends.py:ModelBackend._get_permissions`, `django/contrib/auth/backends.py:ModelBackend.get_all_permissions`).

Within one object a permission given after a check is not seen, even after `Model.refresh_from_db`, which leaves the caches; the documentation's advice is to fetch the user again (`docs/topics/auth/default.txt`):

It asks one backend: the only one configured, or the one whose dotted path it is given, raising `ValueError` when several are configured and none is named (`django/contrib/auth/models.py:UserManager.with_perm`).

`ModelBackend.with_perm` builds one query: the users who hold the permission through a group or directly, or are superusers unless `include_superusers=False`, and who are active unless told otherwise; given an object, no users (`django/contrib/auth/backends.py:ModelBackend.with_perm`).

`AnonymousUser` has the same methods and no superuser shortcut: its `has_perm` and getters ask the backends, and its group permissions are always an empty set (`django/contrib/auth/models.py:AnonymousUser`).

The context processor `django.contrib.auth.context_processors.auth` gives a template `"user"`, the request's user, or an `AnonymousUser` when there is none, and `"perms"`, a `PermWrapper` around that user ([The context: `Context`, `RequestContext` and context processors](../templates/context.md)) (`django/contrib/auth/context_processors.py:auth`).

The `in` of `{% if %}` reaches `PermWrapper.__contains__`, which takes `"fleet.change_ship"` as the same check and `"fleet"` as the application's (`django/contrib/auth/context_processors.py:PermWrapper`).
